summary: Richard Watson recaps the long debate on host names and presents what the NIC hoped would be accepted as an official list of formal host names and nicknames. Hosts chose their own names within agreed guidelines. It was replaced by RFC 384.

plainLanguage.summary: After lots of arguing over nicknames for computers, this is the list everyone hopes to adopt. It was later replaced by a newer list.

subtitle: The official list of ARPANET host names and network addresses for users and systems.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET had no standard way to refer to hosts across different systems. Different sites used different names, making it hard for NCP implementations and Telnet users to specify which computer they wanted.
tldr.mechanism: After a long debate, the NIC collected suggestions from each site and let them choose formal names and nicknames within agreed guidelines, creating a unified registry.
tldr.outcome: RFC 289 presents the negotiated list mapping formal names, nicknames, and network addresses for all ARPANET hosts as of December 1971, but was replaced by RFC 384 as the network grew.

today: RFC 289 was replaced by RFC 384 as the ARPANET expanded and more hosts were added. Today's DNS system provides the same function on the modern internet, but in 1971 this was the authoritative host registry.

sections.title: The Naming Debate
sections.content:
Richard Watson at SRI explains the history of host naming on the ARPANET. The need for standard names had been recognized for years: NCPs (Network Control Programs) and Telnet users needed a consistent way to refer to hosts. Multiple competing name schemes had emerged, causing confusion.

Peggy Karp proposed the first formal standard (RFC 226), followed by counter-proposals and RFC 247. These attempts failed because they did not use names naturally associated with the hosts themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Different places called their computers by different names, so the network couldn't be sure which computer you meant. People couldn't agree on what to call them.

sections.title: The Solution
sections.content:
At an NWG meeting, the consensus emerged that the only workable solution was to support both formal names and nicknames. Guidelines were established (RFC 273), and the NIC invited each site to choose their own formal name and preferred nickname within these guidelines.

The NIC collected the responses, published a tentative list (RFC 280), and refined it as more sites responded. By December 1971, almost all sites had provided their preferred names.
sections.plainLanguage: They decided each site could pick both a fancy name and a short nickname. Everyone sent in their choices, and this list is the result.

sections.title: The Official Registry
sections.content:
RFC 289 lists all ARPANET hosts with three pieces of information for each: the formal name (such as UCLA-NMC or MIT-MULTICS), an optional nickname (such as CCN or MIT-M), and the decimal network address (1 through 158 in this period).

The list covers early ARPANET sites including UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UCSB, Utah, BBN, MIT, RAND, Stanford, Harvard, Lincoln Lab, and many others. Sites were encouraged to change their names in future if the situation warranted.
sections.plainLanguage: The list shows each computer's formal name, its short nickname, and its number on the network. Sites that wanted to rename themselves later could do so.
